content: 1. Sim J and Dawson A explored the ethical considerations of informed consent in cluster-randomized trials, emphasizing the complexities and challenges in obtaining consent in such research designs. Their findings were published in the American Journal of Public Health in 2012. 2. Weijer C, Grimshaw JM, Eccles MP, and colleagues developed the Ottawa Statement, which provides ethical guidelines for the design and conduct of cluster-randomized trials. This statement was published in PLOS Medicine in 2012. 3. Löwy I examined the historical role of the Rockefeller Foundation in Brazil between 1923 and 1939, focusing on its contributions to epidemiology, immunology, and yellow fever control. This analysis was published in the Journal of the History of Biology in 1997. 4. This was detailed in the Dengue Bulletin in 2001. 5. Teng AK and Singh S reviewed the epidemiology of dengue in Malaysia and outlined new initiatives for its prevention and control. Their work was published in the Dengue Bulletin in 2001. 6. Viennet E, Ritchie SA, Williams CR, Faddy HM, and Harley D analyzed public health responses and challenges in controlling dengue transmission in high-income countries through four case studies. Their findings were published in PLOS Neglected Tropical Diseases in 2016. 7. Jamrozik E, Fuente-Núñez V, Reis A, Ringwald P, and Selgelid MJ addressed the ethical aspects of malaria control and research, emphasizing the need for ethical frameworks in disease management. This was published in Malaria Journal in 2015. 8. Gimnig JE, Walker ED, Otieno P, and colleagues investigated the incidence of malaria among mosquito collectors conducting human landing catches in western Kenya, providing insights into occupational risks. Their study appeared in the American Journal of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene in 2013. 9. Achee NL, Youngblood L, Bangs MJ, Lavery JV, and James S developed a tool to guide investigators and regulators on the ethical use of human participants in vector biology research. This was published in Vector-Borne and Zoonotic Diseases in 2015. 10. Lu F, Culleton R, Zhang M, and colleagues reported the emergence of indigenous artemisinin-resistant Plasmodium falciparum in Africa, raising concerns about treatment efficacy. Their findings were published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2017. 11. The World Health Organization (WHO) provided an epidemiological update on yellow fever on March 16, 2017, highlighting recent outbreaks and public health responses. 12. Bambery B, Selgelid M, Weijer C, Savulescu J, and Pollard AJ proposed ethical criteria for conducting human challenge studies in infectious diseases, emphasizing participant safety and scientific integrity. This was published in Public Health Ethics in 2015. 13. Darton TC, Blohmke CJ, Moorthy VS, Altmann DM, Hayden FG, Clutterbuck EA, and colleagues discussed the design, recruitment, and microbiological considerations in human challenge studies, providing a comprehensive framework for such research. Their work appeared in The Lancet Infectious Diseases in 2015. 14. The WHO published regulatory considerations for human challenge trials in vaccine development in 2016, offering guidance for ethical and scientific conduct. 15. Ethical considerations for Zika virus human challenge trials were outlined in a WHO report, which included recommendations for conducting such studies responsibly. 16. McGraw EA and O’Neill SL proposed innovative approaches to vector control beyond traditional insecticides, addressing the challenges of mosquito-borne diseases. Their work was published in Nature Reviews Microbiology in 2013. 17. Hoffmann AA, Montgomery BL, Popovici J, and colleagues successfully established Wolbachia in Aedes mosquito populations to suppress dengue transmission, demonstrating a novel vector control strategy. This was published in Nature in 2011. 18. Jeffery JAL, Yen NT, Nam VS, Hoffmann AA, Kay BH, and Ryan PA characterized Aedes aegypti populations in a Vietnamese village to prepare for a Wolbachia-based mosquito control strategy aimed at eliminating dengue. Their findings were published in PLOS Neglected Tropical Diseases in 2009. 19. Chang MS, Christophel E-M, Gopinath D, and Abdur RM reviewed the challenges and future perspectives for dengue vector control in the Western Pacific Region, emphasizing the need for innovative strategies. This was published in the Western Pacific Surveillance and Response Journal in 2011. 20. The WHO outlined a framework for testing genetically modified mosquitoes, providing guidance for research and implementation. This was published in 2014 as part of the Special Programme for Research and Training in Tropical Diseases. 21. Hirsch F, Lévy Y, and Chneiweiss H presented a European perspective on genome editing technologies, including CRISPR-Cas9, and emphasized the importance of responsible research. This was published in Nature in 2017. 22. Chneiweiss H, Hirsch F, Montoliu L, Müller AM, Fenet S, Abecassis M, and colleagues advocated for fostering responsible research with genome editing technologies, highlighting ethical considerations. Their work appeared in Transgenic Research in 2017. 23. The National Academy of Sciences published a report in 2016 on gene drives, addressing scientific advancements, uncertainties, and the alignment of research with public values. 24. Pugh J examined the ethical implications of eradicating mosquitoes using gene-drive technologies, raising questions about the balance between public health benefits and ecological consequences. This was published in the Journal of Medical Ethics in 2016. 25. The WHO convened a scoping meeting on February 23–24, 2017, to identify ethical issues associated with vector-borne diseases (VBDs). Over 25 international and WHO experts discussed key topics, including environmental and social determinants of health, ethics in vector control (including new technologies), surveillance and research ethics, and the ethics of mass public health interventions. The meeting aimed to address gaps in ethical guidance for VBD control and research, particularly in vulnerable communities.
